text: Nine women, one hundred and fifteen minutes: the arithmetic alone means nobody here gets a full arc. Rodrigo García gives each of them roughly the length of a long phone call, enough time to be interrupted, contradicted or caught out, nowhere near enough to be explained. The premise holds that the bonds sustaining these women are the same ones confining them, which is hard to dramatize without a plot to carry it, so the weight falls on performance, on timing, on what a scene declines to say. Structure like this is a gamble. A segment that fails has nothing to hide behind, and the audience knows within a minute. The Golden Leopard came to it anyway. What accumulates is not a story but a set of pressures, legible to anyone who has been loved and managed by the same person.

A family's entire wealth is alive, on hooves, and it has to be loaded onto a train. Sürü moves that freight across Turkey toward Ankara, and the logic of the trip is merciless: every hour in a sealed wagon is capital dying. A blood feud forced the sale; distance and officialdom do the rest. What the film counts, patiently, are the small extractions along the way, a palm greased here, a head of stock gone missing there, until the sum stops looking like misfortune and starts looking like an arrangement. Travelling with the men is a woman already ill, and her condition sets a second clock against the first. The camera stays at the height of people who cannot afford to stop moving. Sheep do not understand delay. That is the film's cruelty and its clarity.

The black suede shoes come first, and the talent is supposed to arrive later. Tom DiCillo's comedy hands a young man every visible component of a rock and roll idol, the pompadour, the guitar, a couple of friends willing to stand behind him, and none of the invisible ones. Ricky Nelson is the model, an aspiration lifted off a record rather than built from anything he can actually do. Brad Pitt plays him without pleading for sympathy, which is the only way the joke holds: the film neither punishes the pose nor rescues it. Ninety-seven minutes suits a character whose whole life is a stalled first act, long enough to watch the routine repeat, short enough that it stays funny. The production is Swiss, which puts a certain distance between the camera and the American daydream in front of it.

A boy starts his first job, and that is very nearly the whole of the plot. Černý Petr covers a few days of it: instructions half heard, a supervisor to be obeyed, evenings that have to be filled somehow. Miloš Forman keeps to eighty-nine minutes and refuses the usual compensations, since no crisis arrives to give the week a shape and the comedy comes from people talking past each other in rooms where nothing much is at stake. The attention goes elsewhere, to the particular awkwardness of being instructed by adults who are plainly improvising, and to the difference between how a teenager behaves when watched and how he behaves in a crowd. Czechoslovakia in 1964, a shop counter, a first wage. Nothing is dramatized upward. The film lets a small week stay small, which is harder than it sounds.

School lets out in Tehran, the mother does not arrive, and a girl small enough to be overlooked sets off to get home by herself. Jafar Panahi builds ninety-four minutes on that one problem, which means the city has to do the work a plot usually does: buses going the wrong way, adults who are kind for two blocks and then busy, traffic that treats a child as a rounding error. The stakes are not danger exactly, since nobody is hunting her, but the ordinary chance of being lost, which at that age is total. Filming a child through real streets imposes its own honesty: a scene either happens or it does not, and the camera has to keep up rather than arrange things. The Golden Leopard recognized it. What stays afterwards is scale, how a city looks from four feet up and how little of it was built for that height.

A brother and sister were separated by their parents' divorce and have not had to share a room since. Then she runs from boarding school and turns up at his door, and Claire Denis lets the following ninety-nine minutes proceed by proximity rather than argument. Boni bakes pizza for the couple he works for; the mother who preferred him is dead; his days are private and crowded with invented company. Nénette wants none of it explained to her. Denis is interested in what bodies do in a small flat before anyone finds the words, the sulking and the cooking and the doorways stood in too long. What was done to these two stays in the way they move around each other. A problem is coming that neither can defer, and the tact of the film is to let it approach at its own speed.

In this house a sentence can take a full minute to arrive, and the film waits for it. Mike Leigh keeps a secretary at the centre: she looks after her sister, who has an intellectual disability, and is being courted, if that is the word, by a teacher unable to finish a thought in her presence. Around them move a neighbour who is frankly odd and a workmate whose cheerfulness is its own kind of weather. The comedy is genuine and never released. A scene holds well past the point where a joke would ordinarily land, and the discomfort filling those extra seconds is the material. Nothing is heightened; the obstacles are furniture, manners and the length of a pause. What stands to be lost is small and permanent, an evening, then another, then a life arranged around never asking for anything.

A physics student holds that anything worth knowing can be measured, and the film takes ten years to test him on it. Iluminacja compresses that decade into eighty-seven minutes, which forces a particular construction: episodes rather than a plot, each arriving after the last has been left unfinished. Krzysztof Zanussi takes the student's position seriously instead of setting it up to be demolished by feeling. Grief and love interrupt the certainty without being offered as wiser than physics; they are simply facts it cannot absorb. The economy is severe. Eighty-seven minutes is barely enough for one relationship, let alone a decade of them, and the elisions carry most of the argument. Poland, 1973, and a film that assumes an audience will sit through the reasoning, then watch the reasoning fail to cover a life.

The missing man's last known habit was playing a strange video game through the night. He was a Chinese migrant on a Singapore construction site, and the policeman looking for him has that, plus the sleeplessness the search seems to transmit. Yeo Siew Hua lays a detective structure over a labour story and lets the two corrode each other: the genre promises that a disappearance can be solved, while the conditions of the work suggest a man might vanish simply by being replaceable. Ninety-five minutes, Chinese-language, a French production credit on a film about who counts as present in Singapore. A Spanish-language study reads it beside Manta Ray (Puttiphong Aroonpheng, 2018), tracing what the two share. It holds the Golden Leopard, an audience prize at IFFR, and a submission for the international Academy Award.

The two of them keep moving across England because stopping is what would give them away. A man who has killed someone has fallen in with a boy who has run from wherever he was kept, and the arrangement works precisely because neither can say what he wants from it: the child needs company, the man needs the child gone, and both needs go unspoken for the length of the journey. Charles Crichton runs it lean at eighty-four minutes. The road supplies the structure, so nothing has to be explained twice, and the England of 1952 becomes a sequence of places where they cannot stay. Every stranger is a small portrait and a live risk. A film this short has no room for sentiment, and the interest lies in watching the man calculate while the boy, who cannot calculate, simply stays.

A widow watches her son acquire a cause, and the cause has no place in it for her. Silent Waters sets that drift in a Pakistani town near the Indian border, where the young men's new certainty arrives with slogans and a timetable, and where a party of Sikh pilgrims is expected. Sabiha Sumar films the two developments as one weather system: what Saleem is becoming, and what the town is preparing to remember. Ayesha has a past she has kept to herself, and the film lets it stay hers for as long as she can hold it, drawing its tension from proximity rather than disclosure. Ninety-nine minutes, Urdu, a French production behind it. Politics here is not a rally but a household rearranging itself, until a mother finds she is living with someone she has to be careful around.

Two children, one mountain farm, and no neighbours close enough to matter. Höhenfeuer follows a single year of that arrangement: the milking, the weather, the father's temper, a family the valley has nicknamed for its rages. The younger boy is deaf and works like a man, and when his frustration costs the farm an expensive machine he is sent to the far edge of the property, where he breaks rock and builds walls out of it. His sister, who wanted to teach, teaches him. Fredi M. Murer takes two hours and spends them on labour and silence, which is the honest way to film a place nobody visits. The isolation is not standing in for anything. It is the address, and the film is patient enough to let its consequences gather. Switzerland put it forward for the Academy Awards.

A retired mathematics teacher is writing an essay about the beliefs that get people through the day, alone in the flat where his wife used to be. Then a young homeless woman turns up hurt at his door, he keeps her until she can walk again, and the rooms start producing events his manuscript has no line for. Jean-Claude Brisseau stays almost entirely indoors, which suits a horror premise built on argument rather than pursuit. The man has spent a working life on proof; what is happening around him now is exactly the category of thing his essay was written to dissolve. Ninety-one minutes, two people, a few rooms. The interest lies in watching an orderly mind negotiate with a guest it did not invite, and with whatever arrived at the same hour she did.

A man picks fights with everyone in reach because of the one thing he cannot do. Action cinema tends to treat a hero's body as the proof of his worth, and Edwin builds a whole film on a body that withholds the proof, so Ajo Kawir keeps swinging at the world for an answer it does not have. He loses badly to a fighter named Iteung and falls for her on the spot, which turns a brawling picture into a courtship conducted partly with fists. The register keeps shifting: action, romance, a comic timing that undercuts the swagger exactly as it gathers. One hundred and fourteen minutes leaves room for tenderness in between, and the tenderness is not a reversal of the fighting but the reason for it. Machismo gets handled as a medical condition rather than a virtue, and the film is funny about it without cruelty.
